text: You get an array called candidates, and a target. Return all unique combinations that sum to target. Each number may be used only once in a combination. The answer must not contain duplicate combinations.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — once means once per position, right? So if the input has two ones, one, one is a valid combination. But the input itself can have duplicates, and I must not return the same combination twice. And if nothing works, I return an empty list.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and a hundred, each candidate is between one and fifty, and the target is between one and thirty.

Okay. Every value is positive, so a sum only goes up. Once I pass the target, the branch is dead. And the target is at most thirty, so a path is at most thirty numbers deep. Let me run through the example. Ten, one, two, seven, six, one, five with target eight gives one, one, six; one, two, five; one, seven; and two, six. One, one, six uses both ones, and one, seven appears once, even though there are two ones I could pick it with. Two, five, two, one, two with target five gives one, two, two, and five.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to try every subset of indices, keep the ones that hit the target, sort each one, and drop repeats with a set. That's two to the n subsets with n up to a hundred. Way too many, but I'll still use it as a checker on small inputs. This problem reminds me of backtracking with a start index over a sorted array. There are two twists. First, each element is used once, so I recurse with i plus one, not i. Second, the input has duplicates, so I skip equal values on the same level — sorting puts them side by side, which makes that skip a single comparison.

Here's the plan. One: sort the numbers. Two: if the sum equals target, record the path. Three: loop i from s; skip a value equal to the one before it on this level, break once the sum is too big, otherwise push, recurse with i plus one, and pop. I'm using s to keep track of where this level starts. Equal neighbors give the same answers, so each level tries only the first. One thing worth flagging — the check is i greater than s, not i greater than zero. The first index of each level is always allowed; that's how one, one gets built. With i greater than zero, one, one with target two gives nothing. There's a trade-off here. The sort does two jobs: it groups duplicates and makes the break valid. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. The main function sorts, then starts the search with sum zero and start zero. Inside the loop, the dedupe line comes first, then the break, then push, recurse with i plus one, and pop. One thing worth flagging — the sort is a correctness requirement here, not just speed. Without it, both the dedupe and the break go wrong. For example, two, one with target one gives nothing: the loop sees two, breaks, and never looks at one. The order of the two ifs doesn't matter for the result. A skipped duplicate has the same value as the one before it, which already passed the check.
Why not skip the dedupe line and just put the answers in a set at the end? And path is passed by value. Is that OK?

Let me walk through that. A set at the end gives the right answer, but it still has to generate every duplicate first. Take twenty-five ones with target ten. There's only one answer. My code makes 11 calls. Without the dedupe line, it's 7,119,516 calls and 3,268,760 copies of the same answer, about 449 milliseconds. The skip cuts duplicate branches before they start. By value is correct too. Each call gets its own copy, and the pop back undoes the push inside that call, but every call pays for a copy. By reference, there's one shared path, and push and pop keep it clean. On a hundred numbers from one to ten with target thirty, that's 3,239 answers and 19,038 calls: 1.40 milliseconds by value, 0.41 by reference.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Two, five, two, one, two with target five; sorted, it's one, two, two, two, five. Expected: one, two, two, and five. The row that matters is call four, one, two, two, which uses two twos on different levels. Call three picks index two as its first choice, where i equals s, so it's allowed; back in call three, index three is a same-level repeat, so it's skipped. At the root, indices two and three are skipped too. Seven calls, and the result matches. Corner cases: i greater than zero makes one, one, target two return nothing. No dedupe makes one, one, target one return one twice. Recursing with i lets one, target two reuse the same one. No sort makes two, one, target one return nothing. Against the brute force on 8,736 small cases: zero wrong.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is exponential in the worst case, up to two to the n paths. But the dedupe means I never explore the same combination twice, so the real cost is bounded by the number of distinct combinations that still fit under the target, times the copy into the answer, plus n log n for the sort. Space is O of target extra for the recursion stack and the path, since every value is at least one, not counting the output. By value, each level also holds its own copy. In the worst case for duplicates, all ones, the dedupe makes it tiny: a hundred ones with target thirty takes only 31 calls. Oh, one more thing — the dedupe and the break both depend on the sort. If someone optimizes the sort away, the code doesn't just get slower. It returns wrong answers.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You explained why it's i greater than s, not i greater than zero — same level versus deeper level — with one, one, target two as proof. You knew the sort does two jobs: grouping duplicates and making the break valid. And you measured the dedupe: 11 calls versus 7,119,516 on the all-ones case, plus by value versus by reference. Good work.
